title: The Lethal Mutation of Retrieval Practice
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick writes what many in the science-of-learning community have been circling but slow to name: retrieval practice, the celebrated testing effect, has boundary conditions, and the evidence-informed movement has blown past them. The piece anchors on a 2025 Redifer study that gave undergraduates a real 2500-word psychology journal article rather than the word-pair lists or short passages where the testing effect was established. Retrieval practice produced no advantage over rereading. Bayesian analysis placed the null result at roughly seven times more likely than a meaningful group difference, and cognitive load fully mediated the effect: the retrieval effort was overwhelming memory rather than strengthening it. From that single study Hendrick builds the argument he has been quietly forming for years, which is that retrieval practice is becoming a lethal mutation, borrowing the Wiliam and Jones phrase for an evidence-based practice distorted in the field until it is a pale imitation of itself. He then lays out five principles for keeping the mutation at bay. You cannot retrieve from memory what never made it into memory, so retrieval belongs after initial learning, not during it. Retrieval without curriculum is just activity, strengthening whatever is retrieved regardless of whether it is load-bearing or trivia. Not all knowledge is retrievable in the same way: discrete declarative knowledge is retrievable; integrative, relational, or constructed understanding is not in the same sense. Single retrievals are not the testing effect; spacing, and return across expanding intervals, is what produces it. And effort is not a free resource, so the desirable difficulty of retrieval practice collapses when the cognitive load of comprehension has already consumed the learner's capacity. The move for primary and secondary teachers is clear. Retrieval practice is a consolidation strategy, not a comprehension strategy. It strengthens traces; it does not build them. The practical implications are sequential (comprehension first, consolidation second), curricular (know what is worth retrieving before you design the quiz), typological (discriminate between declarative facts and integrative arguments), architectural (build spaced return into the course rather than closing each topic), and capacity-aware (do not layer retrieval on top of material that already demands everything the learner has). The strategy still works. What has to change is where and when it is deployed.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: A lethal mutation is an idea or a practice that is prompted by sound scientific evidence, but is implemented in a way that reduces, or even completely negates, its effectiveness.

Retrieval practice is a consolidation strategy, not a comprehension strategy. It works when learners already have something in memory worth retrieving. It strengthens existing traces; it does not build them.

When students are still grappling with understanding, when they are still constructing the schema that will eventually be worth consolidating, asking them to retrieve is asking them to lift weights they haven’t yet built the muscles for.
There is a version of retrieval practice that strengthens memory, and a version that overwhelms it. The difference lies in what the learner brings to the task.

Retrieval practice strengthens whatever is retrieved. It does not discriminate between the essential and the trivial. This is a feature when retrieval practice is well designed but it becomes a serious problem when it is not.
The curriculum must decide what the signal is before retrieval amplifies it.
That single quiz was not retrieval practice. It was assessment. It measured what students knew at that moment; it did not change what they would know later.

The strategy doesn’t fail because it’s ineffective. It fails because it’s being applied outside the conditions that make it effective.” Archived from The Learning Dispatch (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
